1000504.etyen: Borrowed from French Mars (“Mars, a commune in Ardèche”). The commune was called Saint-Romain-le-Désert until 1909, when it adopted the name of the older and more populous hamlet of Mars. According to the French cultural-heritage inventory, the hamlet's name may derive from a Roman temple dedicated to the god Mārs (“Mars”) beside the Roman road that crossed the area.

en.g: a female given name, a feminine derivative of Hans

1001272.etyen:
From Hans (“male given name”) + -ine (“feminine name-forming suffix”). Names of this type became fashionable in Norway in the 18th century, having been transmitted through Danish from German, and were chiefly used when daughters were named after male relatives. The base name Hans is a German short form of Johannes, which comes via Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs) from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”).
First attested in the 18th century in Norway.

1004856.etyen:
Probably a calque of Dutch BES-eilanden (“BES Islands”). The initialism is formed from the first letters of Bonaire, (Sint) Eustatius and Saba.
The final element, øyene (“the islands”), is the definite plural of øy (“island”), inherited from Old Norse ey (“island”), from Proto-Germanic *awjō (“floodplain, meadow, island”), from earlier *agwjō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ékʷeh₂ (“water”).
Parallel formations include Dutch BES-eilanden, Danish BES-øerne, German BES-Inseln and English BES Islands.

en.g: a mild oath, expletive, or exclamation, roughly damn, damn it, or wow, used to express disgust, irritation, surprise, admiration, strong enthusiasm, or being overwhelmed
x: Fyttekatta, så kaldt det er ute!

1005112.etyen:
Contraction of fy (“fie, shame”) + til (“to”) + katta (“the cat”), literally “fie to the cat”.
The first element, fy (“fie, shame”), is imitative, originally representing a spitting sound. The final element is the feminine definite singular of katt (“cat”), from Old Norse kǫttr (“cat”), from Late Latin cattus (“cat”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk fyttikatta (“mild oath, exclamation”) and Swedish fy katten (“damn, darn”).
